Report Errors in the PDF - support@careerscloud.in Copyright 2014-2026 @ AffairsCloud.com 14 Daily Content PDF NATIONAL AFFAIRS CBIC Notifies Key GST Changes under Finance Act, 2026 Effective from November 01, 2026 In October 2026, the Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs (CBIC), a statutory body under the Department of Revenue (DoR), Ministry of Finance (MoF), issued a notification in exercise of powers given under Section 1(2)(b) of the Finance Act, 2026, and appointed November 01, 2026 as the date on which the key Goods and Services Tax (GST) changes introduced under the Act will come into force. • The key GST changes are related to the treatment of post-sale discounts; provisional refunds under the inverted duty structure, aimed at easing compliance and enhancing liquidity flow for businesses. Exam Hints: ✓ What? Notification of Effective Date for Key GST Amendments ✓ Notified by: CBIC, MoF ✓ Effective from: November 01, 2026 ✓ GST Amendments Through: Finance Act, 2026 ✓ Key Changes: Post-Supply Discounts, Credit Notes, Provisional Refunds and Export Refund Threshold ✓ Provisional Refund: Up to 90% of Eligible Refund Amount ✓ Export Refund Relaxation: Removal of Rs 1,000 Minimum Threshold Key GST Changes: Post-Supply Discounts: The amended section 15 (3)(b) of the Act introduced the provision to exclude post- supply discounts from the value of supply if the supplier issues a credit note and the recipient reverses the corresponding Input Tax Credit (ITC), without the requirement of prior agreement or strict invoice-wise linkage. Credit Notes: Section aligned with the statutory provisions under Section 34(1) of the Central Goods, Services and Tax (CGST Act, 2017) to explicitly cover post-supply discounts as a valid ground for issuing GST credit notes. Provisional Refunds for Inverted Duty Structure: Section 54(6) of the Act extends the statutory provisional refund mechanism to eligible inverted duty structure claims, enabling businesses to receive 90% of eligible refunds provisionally within 7 days, subject to conditions. Removal of Export Refund Limit: In addition, the amended section 54(14) removes the Rs 1,000 minimum refund restriction for tax paid on goods exported out of India, benefiting small exporters. • However, this relaxation is not applicable to other refund categories. Background: Union Budget 2026–27: The GST amendments were proposed in the Union Budget for Financial Year 2026–27 (FY27), presented by Union Minister Nirmala Sitharaman, Ministry of Finance, on 1 February 2026. About Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs (CBIC): Chairman- Vivek Chaturvedi Headquarters- New Delhi, Delhi Established in- 1964 GoI Constitutes High-Level Committee on Banking for Viksit Bharat, Chaired by Suresh N. Report Errors in the PDF - support@careerscloud.in Copyright 2014-2026 @ AffairsCloud.com 15 Daily Content PDF High-Level Committee on Banking for Viksit Bharat, chaired by Suresh N. Patel, former Central Vigilance Commissioner (CVC), with a tenure of six months. • The newly formed committee has been tasked to undertake a comprehensive review of the country’s banking sector and recommend structural, institutional, regulatory and legislative reforms to make it globally competitive, financially inclusive and resilient for Viksit Bharat, 2047. Exam Hints: ✓ What? Constitution of High-Level Committee on Banking for Viksit Bharat ✓ Announced by: MoF ✓ Chaired by: Suresh N. Patel, formed CVC ✓ Tenure: Six months ✓ Members: Shirish Chandra Murmu, Padmaja Chunduru and N. S. Vishwanathan ✓ Member Secretary: Joint Secretary (Banking), DFS, MoF Key Details of the Committee: Background: In February 2026, While presenting the Union Budget for Financial Year 2026-27 (FY27), Union Minister Nirmala Sitharaman, Ministry of Finance (MoF), announced the setting up of the committee. Composition: Apart from the charmain, the committee comprises members that include: Shirish Chandra Murmu, Deputy Governor, Reserve Bank of India (RBI); Padmaja Chunduru, former Managing Director (MD) & Chief Executive Officer (CEO) of Indian Bank; and N S Vishwanathan, former Deputy Governor, RBI. • In addition, the Joint Secretary (Banking), Department of Financial Services (DFS), MoF, has been appointed as the Member Secretary of the committee. Terms of Reference (ToR): Review of Banking Regulations: The committee will examine the existing regulatory and legislative frameworks governing banks, including Regional Rural Banks (RRBs) and cooperative banks, and recommend reforms to strengthen the banking system. Global Banking Practices: It will assess existing banking practices and prudential norms, identify international best practices and prepare a roadmap for developing globally competitive banks. Capital Requirements: The committee will evaluate the long-term capital requirements of banks, Development Financial Institutions (DFIs) and Non-Banking Financial Companies (NBFCs) to support India’s growing economy. Cost of Capital: It will examine differences in the cost of capital for businesses and recommend measures to encourage private investment and sustainable economic growth. Emerging Technologies: The committee will prepare a roadmap for adopting Artificial Intelligence (AI) and digital innovation in banking institutions, along with safeguards against cybersecurity risks. Talent Acquisition: It will recommend measures for talent acquisition, skill development and capacity building to create a future-ready banking workforce. Financial Inclusion: The committee will review the Priority Sector Lending (PSL) framework and Lead Bank Scheme (LBS) to assess their relevance, effectiveness and coordination in promoting inclusive, balanced and data-driven credit delivery. Additional Mandate: The committee may also examine other banking-related matters referred to it by the GoI.

Highlights of the National Social Security Board: Composition: The Unorganised Workers’ Board includes representatives from trade unions, employers’ organisations, civil society, Members of Parliament (MPs), Central Ministries and State Governments, with the Director General (DG) of Labour Welfare as its ex-officio Member-Secretary. • The Gig and Platform Workers’ Board includes five aggregators, Eternal Group, Swiggy, Zepto, Urban Company and Rapido, and worker representatives from the Indian Federation of App- Based Transport Workers (IFAT), Bharatiya Mazdoor Sangh (BMS), National Front of Indian Trade Unions (NFITU) and Trade Union Coordination Centre (TUCC). Functions: The boards recommend suitable social security schemes, advise the Central Government on Code-related matters, monitor centrally administered welfare schemes, review State-level record-keeping and expenditure from relevant funds and accounts, and perform other functions assigned by the Centre. Framework: The Code on Social Security, 2020, was enacted in September 2020, came into effect on 21 November 2025 and replaced nine central labour laws; Section 6 establishes the National Social Security Board for unorganised workers, while Section 114(6) assigns its responsibilities concerning gig and platform workers through separate membership. Categories: Gig workers earn through arrangements outside the traditional employer–employee relationship, whereas platform workers undertake work through or with online platforms, including food- delivery and ride-hailing applications. About Six Selected Start-ups: Funding: With an outlay of up to Rs. 6 crore, the programme supports startups and Micro and Small Enterprises (MSEs) in developing indigenous AI-based space technologies across three areas: Edge Intelligence in Orbit, Space for Earth Intelligence and Smart Access to Space. Selected Start-ups: The six selected entities are Agnikul Cosmos (AI-based precision landing), Digantara (space object evaluation), EON Space Labs (space debris detection), OrbitAid Aerospace (satellite servicing and refuelling), Omnipresent Robot Technologies (automated target recognition for defence and docking) and TakeMeToSpace (AI-based spacecraft autonomy and control).

INTERNATIONAL AFFAIRS World Bank Report: India Records One of the World’s Fastest Poverty Declines in 12 Years, to 2.6% In October 2026, the World Bank (WB) released its latest report titled “India Poverty and Equity Brief: October 2026”, highlighting that India’s extreme poverty rate declined from 27.1% in 2011 to 2.6% in 2023, marking one of the fastest poverty reductions globally over 12 years. • The report estimated that 496 million people moved above the lower-middle-income poverty threshold of USD 4.20 per day, measured using 2021 Purchasing Power Parity (PPP). Exam Hints: ✓ What? Release of report titled “Poverty and Equity Belief: October 2026” ✓ Released by: World Bank ✓ Period Covered: 2011–2023 (12 years) ✓ Extreme Poverty Rate in India: Declined from 27.1% to 2.6% (between 2011 and 2023) ✓ Extreme Poverty Line: USD 3 per day (2021 PPP) ✓ People Lifted Above USD 4.20 Poverty Line: 496 million ✓ Key Drivers: robust consumption growth, improvement in employment; and expanded social transfers (including food subsidies) ✓ Non-monetary Poverty Rate: 16.4% (2019-21). Key Findings: Key Drivers: The report cited that the poverty rate decline was mainly attributed to the robust consumption growth, improvement in employment, particularly women; and expanded social transfers, including food subsidies. LMI Poverty Line: Also, the proportion of people living below the Lower-Middle-Income Country (LMIC) poverty line of USD 4.20 per day (measured at 2021 Purchasing Power Parity, PPP), declined from 57.7% to 16.1% during the period. Key Projection: The report further projected that the poverty rate (at the USD 4.20 per day threshold) could decline in the next 2 years, although at a slower pace i.e. from 14.2% (in 2026) to 12.1% (by 2028). Non-monetary Poverty: As per the WB’s latest report, non-monetary poverty, which is measured through the Oxford Poverty and Human Development Initiative (OPHI)’s Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI) has also decreased from 53.8% (in 2005-06) to 16.4% (2019-21). • The report also showed that WB’s multidimensional poverty measure stood at 15.5% (in 2022- 23). Gini Index: The WB reported India’s Gini Index at 23.0 in 2023, measuring income or consumption inequality on a scale of 0 to 100, where 0 indicates perfect equality and 100 represents maximum inequality. Geographical Poverty Disparities: In 2023, poverty at the USD 4.20-per-day threshold was higher in rural areas (19.3%) than in urban areas (8.6%), with around 57% of India’s poor population concentrated in a belt stretching from Uttar Pradesh (UP) to West Bengal (WB). Key Challenges: However, the report outlined some of the key factors that could impede the poverty rate decline such as: regional and employment-related challenges.
